content: Lithium nitride is a chemical compound composed of lithium and nitrogen, with the molecular formula Li₃N. It is the only stable nitride of the alkali metals. In its solid state, lithium nitride appears as a red or purple material, characterized by a high melting point and ionic bonding. Its crystal structure is unique, consisting of two distinct types of layers: one layer, with the composition Li₂N, contains lithium ions in a six-coordinate arrangement, while the other layer is composed solely of lithium ions. Solid lithium nitride exhibits remarkable ionic conductivity, making it the fastest ion conductor among all inorganic lithium salts. This property has led to extensive research into its potential applications as a solid electrolyte and as an anode material in battery technologies. Lithium nitride can be synthesized through the direct reaction of lithium and nitrogen. This can be achieved by burning lithium metal in pure nitrogen gas or by reacting nitrogen gas with lithium dissolved in liquid sodium metal. The latter method yields a product of higher purity. When lithium nitride comes into contact with water, it reacts violently, producing ammonia gas and lithium hydroxide in aqueous solution, as shown in the reaction: Li₃N (s) + 3 H₂O (l) → 3 LiOH (aq) + NH₃ (g) This behavior is typical of ionic nitrides, as the N³⁻ ion is an exceptionally strong Brønsted base. It qualifies as a superbase, being even stronger than the hydride ion (H⁻). As a result, lithium nitride can deprotonate molecular hydrogen, as demonstrated in the following reaction: Li₃N (s) + 2 H₂ (g) → LiNH₂ (s) + 2 LiH (s) Lithium nitride is also being explored as a potential medium for hydrogen gas storage. The reaction between lithium nitride and hydrogen is reversible at a temperature of 270°C, and the material has demonstrated the ability to absorb up to 11.5% of its weight in hydrogen. This property makes it a promising candidate for hydrogen storage applications.
